nameStory: The elegant spreadwing gets its name from the graceful way it holds its wings when at rest - spreading them horizontally out from its body rather than folding them back like most damselflies do. The 'elegant' part refers to its slender build and refined appearance, giving it an almost delicate, aristocratic look among the damselflies.
description: The elegant spreadwing is a medium-sized damselfly with a slender, delicate build typical of the spreadwing family. Like all spreadwings, it holds its wings horizontally when perched rather than folded along its body like most damselflies. Adults typically measure about 1.5-2 inches long with a narrow body that's usually bronze or brownish in color. You'll spot them near ponds, marshes, and slow-moving waters throughout the warmer months.

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: Wings held horizontally outward when at rest, not folded back along the body like most damselflies - this spread-wing posture is the signature feature of the entire family

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Slender bronze to brownish body with a metallic sheen that catches the light, feeling smooth and slightly waxy to the touch if gently handled

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Medium-sized with an especially delicate, narrow build - about as thick as a thin pencil and roughly 1.5-2 inches long from head to tail

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Weak, fluttery flight that looks almost hesitant compared to the strong, direct flight of dragonflies - often stays close to vegetation

idTips.label: Perching Behavior
idTips.description: Often perches vertically on plant stems or cattails with wings spread, looking like a tiny airplane viewed from above

habitat: Look for elegant spreadwings around ponds, marshes, slow streams, and other calm freshwater areas with plenty of emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. They prefer areas with some shallow, weedy sections where aquatic plants grow up through the water surface. You'll often find them in marshy edges of lakes or in beaver ponds throughout New England's lowlands and valleys.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but early season sightings are uncommon. Any spreadwings seen in May are likely overwintered individuals from the previous year.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most abundant and actively mating. Look for them perched on vegetation near water during warm, calm days from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active well into fall, often until the first hard frosts. This is when you might spot late-season mating and egg-laying behavior.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - they spend winter as eggs or larvae underwater in ponds and marshes, completely hidden from view.

funFact: Unlike most damselflies that lay their eggs directly in water, elegant spreadwings often insert their eggs into plant stems above the waterline, where the eggs must survive through winter and won't hatch until spring floods or rising water levels reach them!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other spreadwing species in the same genus, all of which share the distinctive horizontal wing posture. The key is looking at subtle differences in body coloration and size - elegant spreadwings tend to have a more bronze coloration compared to the greener emerald spreadwings or the more amber-toned amber-winged spreadwings.
contextualKnowledge: The spreadwing family gets overlooked by many people who assume all damselflies fold their wings back when resting. Once you learn to spot the horizontal wing position, you'll start noticing spreadwings everywhere - they're much more common than most people realize.
compareHints: Among New England's spreadwings, the elegant spreadwing is distinguished by its bronze-brown coloration and medium size. It's larger than the slender spreadwing but smaller than the robust swamp spreadwing, and lacks the distinctive green metallic sheen of the emerald spreadwing. The amber-winged spreadwing has more yellowish wing tints, while the elegant has clearer wings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's spreadwings, the Slender Spreadwing is distinguished by its exceptionally thin body profile and pale blue face coloration.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Spotted Spreadwing is one of the easier ones to identify thanks to its distinctive wing spots.
Among New England's nine Lestes species, Swamp Spreadwings are distinguished by their strong preference for heavily vegetated wetlands and their larger, more robust build.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Amber-winged is distinguished by its wing coloration when present, though this can be subtle.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Northern Spreadwing is distinguished by its preference for more permanent water bodies compared to species like the Swamp Spreadwing which favors temporary pools.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Emerald Spreadwing stands out for its brilliant metallic green coloration - most others like the Swamp Spreadwing appear more bronze or brown.
Among New England spreadwings, sweetflag spreadwings are distinguished by their preference for heavily vegetated wetlands rather than open water.
